opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting directions right now. Video generation models have gotten remarkably good at producing realistic, coherent clips, but for the most part you're a passive viewer: you give a prompt and watch what comes out. The question I find really compelling is how to turn that into something you can actually step into and act within, where the scene responds to what you do frame by frame.

One of the big challenges is that most of the video on the internet doesn't come with action labels. You have enormous amounts of footage of people playing games, moving through environments, manipulating objects, but nobody wrote down which button was pressed or which motor command was issued at each step. So a lot of the interesting work is figuring out how to learn a notion of action without supervision, essentially inferring latent actions from the changes you see between consecutive frames. If you can learn a compact, consistent action space that way, you can then let a user, or an agent, choose those actions and have the model generate what happens next.

Once you have that, the potential is pretty broad. On the creative side, you could imagine someone sketching an image or describing a world and then immediately being able to play in it, which opens up new ways of prototyping games and interactive experiences. On the research side, and this is the part I'm personally most excited about, these models become a kind of generative world model for training agents. One of the big bottlenecks in reinforcement learning and embodied AI is the lack of rich, diverse environments. If you can generate an essentially unlimited range of controllable environments from video, you get a much richer curriculum for training more general agents.

There are still real open problems. Consistency over long horizons is hard; things can drift or the model can forget what was off-screen. Making controls feel responsive and precise, rather than loosely correlated with what you intended, is another. And there's a question of how well latent actions learned from one domain transfer to another. But I think the trajectory is clear: we're moving from models that generate video to models that generate worlds you can interact with, and that shift unlocks a lot.

r001.rationale: It describes moving from passive video generation to scenes users can enter and control, with the scene responding to actions frame by frame.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a dog-control approach, a 2D platformer, or doubt about whether that approach would work in 3D.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the most exciting directions in the space right now, and it's something I've been thinking about for a while because it connects pretty directly to the work I did on Genie and some of the earlier stuff in reinforcement learning around learning from videos.

So if you think about where video generation has been, it's mostly been a passive thing. You give it a prompt, it gives you a clip, and that's the end of the interaction. It's beautiful, it's getting really photorealistic, but it's fundamentally a one-shot generation. What interactive control does is turn that into something closer to a world model, or really a playable environment. Now instead of just watching the scene, you can say "move the character left," or "open that door," and the model has to generate what happens next conditioned on your action.

The thing I find really interesting is where those actions come from. In a lot of traditional approaches, you'd need labeled action data, so someone annotating "at this frame the player pressed jump." That doesn't scale, because the internet is full of video but almost none of it has action labels attached. So one of the key ideas we explored was learning a latent action space in an unsupervised way. You look at consecutive frames and ask, what's the minimal piece of information that explains the transition from this frame to the next? And it turns out you can learn a small discrete set of codes that end up corresponding to meaningful, controllable things, like moving in a direction or jumping, even though nobody ever told the model what those actions were.

Once you have that, a bunch of doors open up. One is obviously games and creative tools, where someone sketches a scene or takes a photo and suddenly it's a little world they can walk around in. But the one I care about maybe even more is for training agents. If you can generate an interactive environment from a single image or a text description, you've essentially got an unlimited supply of diverse training environments. Agents can practice in them, learn policies, and then transfer to the real thing. That's been a dream in RL for a long time, and generative video with control starts to make it feel plausible.

There are real challenges, though. Consistency over long horizons is a big one. If I walk through a door and then turn around, the room I just left should still be there, and models still struggle with that kind of memory. There's also the question of how faithful the dynamics are. It's easy to get something that looks right for a few frames but doesn't actually respect physics or the rules of the environment, and if you're training agents on that, you can learn the wrong things. And then there's latency, because for it to feel interactive it has to run at something close to real time, which is a very different constraint than generating a polished clip offline.

But I think the trajectory is pretty clear. We're moving from video as a thing you watch to video as a thing you can inhabit and act in, and I think that shift is going to matter a lot, both for how people create and for how we build and train intelligent systems.

r001.rationale: The response says interactive control turns generated clips into playable environments where users can issue actions such as moving a character or opening a door.

r002.rationale: The response does not express doubt about a dog-control approach demonstrated in a 2D platformer working in 3D.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a really exciting direction. Instead of generating a video that you just watch, imagine being able to take an action within that scene and have the video respond. Could you move through the environment, pick something up, or change what happens next? That starts to look like an interactive world rather than a fixed sequence of frames.

The challenge is making those interactions consistent. A scene can look convincing, but if you move away and come back, do the same objects still exist? If you push something, does it respond in a way that makes sense? If we can get those things right, there’s a lot of potential for using these environments to train agents and let them explore different outcomes.

r001.rationale: It describes taking actions within a generated scene and having the video respond, adding interactive control beyond simply watching the generated video.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a really exciting direction. Instead of generating a video that you can only watch, imagine being able to take an action within that scene and have the video respond. You could move through the environment, interact with objects, or change what happens next.

The challenge is that looking realistic isn’t enough. The system has to respond consistently to your actions and maintain that consistency over time. If you move something and then look away, it should still be where you left it when you turn back. If we can get that right, these models could become useful interactive environments for training and evaluating agents, as well as for people to explore.
